findings.summary: The SEC-3 consequence overclaims that envelope-metadata tampering is detected, contradicting the security-review source of record.
findings.detail: The new SEC-3 entry states: 'metadata tampering is detected by the version/authority handling, not by the hash.' The source of record (docs/implementation/final-review/security-review.json, finding SEC-3) makes the opposite point: the envelope metadata is NOT covered by the hash and 'Retention trusts the unauthenticated Terminal and UpdatedUtc fields'; it never claims metadata tampering is detected, and its stated guarantee is 'corruption detection rather than tamper authentication'. Code inspection confirms the overclaim: StateEnvelopeCodec.TryReadEnvelope rejects only a mismatched SchemaVersion (lines 144-149); the Kind, RecordId, and Authority fields are never validated (StateRepository.Read discards the parsed envelope and derives paths from caller arguments, StateRepository.cs:58-83), and Terminal/UpdatedUtc are read and trusted by StateRetention.IsTerminalAndExpired (StateRetention.cs:164). So the sentence is false for five of the six metadata fields and, by implying metadata tampering is caught, understates the very limitation SEC-3 records. This violates the task's explicit requirement of accurate consequence wording with no overclaim.
findings.recommended_action: Reword the first sentence of the SEC-3 '- Consequence:' bullet to mirror security-review.json SEC-3: the SHA-256 covers only PayloadJson; SchemaVersion is the only separately validated metadata field; Terminal/UpdatedUtc are trusted by retention; therefore StateEnvelopeCodec is a corruption detector, not a tamper MAC.
